Britannica Editors Last updated July 30, 2026 •History Britannica AI Ask Anything Quick Summary Table of Contents Table of Contents Quick Summary Ask Anything Top Questions What is the human respiratory system? The human respiratory system facilitates the continuous exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between the body and the environment. This vital process involves two main mechanisms: convection and diffusion. The system consists of the upper and lower airway systems. The upper airway includes the nose, paranasal cavities, pharynx, and oral cavity. The lower airway comprises the larynx, trachea, stem bronchi, intrapulmonary bronchi, bronchioles, and alveolar ducts. The diaphragm, the main respiratory muscle, along with the intercostal muscles, facilitates the pumping action of the lungs. Blood and the circulatory system are essential for gas transport. 3 Britannica Sources childhood disease and disorder: Respiratory disorders human respiratory system: The intrapulmonary conducting airways: bronchi and bronchioles diaphragm This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. How does the human body take in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide? The human respiratory system facilitates the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide through ventilation and diffusion. Air enters the lungs, where oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood and binds to hemoglobin in red blood cells. Simultaneously, carbon dioxide moves from the blood into the alveoli to be exhaled. This diffusion is driven by differences in partial pressures: oxygen moves from the air into the blood, while carbon dioxide moves from the blood into the air. The blood transports these gases between the lungs and the body's tissues. 2 Britannica Sources 13 Questions About How the Human Body Works Answered: How do people breathe in and out? human respiratory system: Gas exchange in the lung This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. What are the main organs involved in breathing? The primary organs involved in breathing work together to supply the body with oxygen and expel carbon dioxide. Lungs The lungs are the main organs for gas exchange. Within the lungs, oxygen and carbon dioxide move between the air and the blood across the respiratory exchange surfaces. Diaphragm This dome-shaped muscle located below the lungs is essential for breathing. When it contracts, the diaphragm increases the height of the thoracic cavity, which lowers the pressure inside and causes air to flow into the lungs. Trachea The trachea, or windpipe, is a tube that carries air from the larynx to the lungs. Bronchi The trachea divides into two main bronchi that enter the lungs. These bronchi further divide into smaller and narrower airways called bronchioles, which distribute air to the gas-exchanging zone of the lung. 6 Britannica Sources pulmonary alveolus trachea bronchus human skeleton: The rib cage human respiratory system: The trachea and the stem bronchi diaphragm This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. What is the process of gas exchange in the lungs? In the lungs, gas exchange occurs across respiratory exchange surfaces between air and blood. The structure of the human lung provides a large internal surface area with a thin membrane that enhances gas exchange between the alveoli and pulmonary capillaries. The process of diffusion drives gas exchange, moving gases from areas of higher partial pressure to lower partial pressure. Oxygen and carbon dioxide are transported between tissue cells and the lungs via blood. The efficiency of gas exchange relies on the uniform distribution of blood flow and inspired air throughout the lungs. 1 Britannica Source human respiratory system: Gas exchange in the lung This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. How do the diaphragm and intercostal muscles help with breathing? The diaphragm and intercostal muscles facilitate breathing through mechanical actions that change the volume of the chest cavity. The diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscle separating the chest and abdominal cavities, contracts and moves downward to increase the chest cavity's height, which lowers the internal pressure and draws air into the lungs. The external intercostal muscles contract, lifting the ribs up and outward to expand the chest circumference. During expiration, these muscles relax, and the chest wall and lungs' elastic recoil force air out. The internal intercostal muscles depress the rib cage to decrease chest circumference during labored breathing or exercise. 3 Britannica Sources respiratory system: Mammals human skeleton: The rib cage diaphragm This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. Breathing rate and depth are automatically controlled by neuron networks in the hindbrain, specifically the pons and medulla. These networks manage the muscles in the thorax and abdomen, creating pressure gradients for air movement in and out of the lungs. The respiratory system adjusts breathing patterns based on internal and external changes via sensors throughout the body. Chemoreceptors identify changes in blood oxygen levels and acidity, while mechanoreceptors monitor lung expansion and muscle contraction. news.content_zh: 该文章来自布拉提卡,讨论了季节性流感病毒及其全球影响,重点聚焦于大流行病的准备。文章概述了世界卫生组织(WHO)的六阶段大流行病警报系统,包括对潜在大流行病早期迹象的监测,例如孤立的动物到人类的传播。文本解释了随着病毒传播并在多个国家引发持续的人类到人类的传播,警报级别会提高,从而导致更紧迫的缓解措施。文章描述了流感是一种影响所有年龄段的疾病,尽管在儿童和年轻人中更为常见。文章还指出,流感暴发在较冷的月份更为频繁,可能导致严重的并发症,如肺炎或支气管炎,这些并发症可能致命,尤其是在老年人中。此外,文章还提到了抗病毒药物抗病毒药物,如奥司他韦和扎那米韦,这些药物对甲型和乙型流感病毒均有效,并指出病毒抗药性已降低了某些治疗的有效性。文章未报告特定的暴发或确诊病例,但提供了关于流感传播、症状和预防策略的一般信息。

news.content_title: GSK’s mRNA Flu Vaccine Heads to Phase III
news.content: Close Menu Facebook X (Twitter) Instagram Facebook Instagram Threads Subscribe Featured Ebola Outbreak Avian Influenza Measles Resurgence Vaccine News Events Advertisement Medical Countermeasures GSK’s mRNA Flu Vaccine Heads to Phase III Dual-antigen approach could raise the bar in a market already transformed by Moderna's recent mRNA approval By Global Biodefense StaffSeptember 2, 2026 Flu virus particles. Credit: NIAID Share Facebook LinkedIn Reddit Email A new generation of influenza vaccines may be taking shape. GSK announced on Sept. 1, 2026, that it will advance its investigational mRNA seasonal flu vaccine candidate into a pivotal Phase III trial following positive Phase II results presented at the OPTIONS XIII Conference for the Control of Influenza in Washington, D.C. The trial is set to begin this month. The development arrives just weeks after Moderna secured U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval for mFlusiva, the first mRNA influenza vaccine to reach market, approved on Aug. 5 for adults 50 and older. GSK’s candidate is pursuing a different and potentially broader strategy, one that has not yet been tested in a Phase III trial anywhere in the world. A Two-Target Strategy Most licensed flu vaccines, including Moderna’s newly approved mFlusiva, focus on hemagglutinin (HA), the protein that allows the flu virus to attach to and enter human cells. GSK’s candidate, designated FLUm3HA.b-3NA, is designed to also target neuraminidase (NA), the protein responsible for helping newly replicated virus particles spread from infected cells to healthy ones. Growing evidence suggests that engaging NA alongside HA could improve protection, reduce illness severity, and limit transmission. No approved flu vaccine currently takes this dual approach. In the Flu-028 Phase II trial, a randomized, observer-blind study enrolling 971 adults aged 18 and older, GSK’s vaccine candidate generated higher immune responses against all influenza strains tested compared to licensed standard-dose and high-dose inactivated flu vaccines, in younger and older adult groups respectively. The trial assessed immunogenicity and safety data through day 181 post-vaccination. GSK has not yet released the underlying numerical data publicly; detailed results were shared in an oral presentation at the OPTIONS XIII conference. The FDA granted GSK’s candidate Fast Track designation in July 2026 for its targeted age indication, a regulatory tool used to expedite development of therapies addressing unmet medical needs. An Evolving and Competitive Landscape Seasonal influenza causes approximately one billion infections annually, including up to five million severe cases and up to 650,000 respiratory deaths worldwide, according to the World Health Organization. Conventional flu vaccines have shown variable effectiveness ranging from roughly 20 to 60 percent over the past 15 years, leaving substantial room for improvement. Moderna’s mFlusiva demonstrated approximately 26.6 percent greater effectiveness at preventing laboratory-confirmed influenza compared to traditional vaccines in clinical trials, with a stronger immune response in adults 65 and older. The vaccine has been tested in roughly 70,000 clinical trial participants and is now entering its first real-world flu season, with questions about pricing, availability, and uptake still unresolved. GSK’s entry into Phase III positions it as a second-mover in the mRNA flu space, but with a differentiated scientific rationale. Moderna had previously explored HA and NA dual-targeting in its own pipeline but paused that work amid broader pipeline reprioritization. GSK is now carrying that hypothesis forward into late-stage testing. news.content: Skip to main content News Entertainment Weather Galleries Sports Watch Live Now 77° Tue 83° Wed 80° Live1 FDA updates this season's flu shot; Bronson doctor urges early flu prep by Princess Jhané Stepherson|NewsChannel3 Wed, September 2, 2026 at 4:43 PM Updated Wed, September 2, 2026 at 6:05 PM Play/Pause Video Quality Speed0.25x0.5xnormal1.5x2x Audio Track Audio Quality Subtitlesopen Font sizedefault50%75%100%150%200%300%400% Font styledefaultitalicbold Font familydefaultmonospaced serifproportional serifmonospaced sans serifproportional sans serifcasualcursivesmall capital Font colordefaultwhiteblackredgreenbluecyanyellowmagenta Font opacitydefault100%75%50%25% Character edgedefaultraiseddepresseduniformdrop shadowed Character edge colordefaultwhiteblackredgreenbluecyanyellowmagenta Background colordefaultwhiteblackredgreenbluecyanyellowmagenta Background opacitydefault100%75%50%25%0% Window colordefaultwhiteblackredgreenbluecyanyellowmagenta Window opacitydefault100%75%50%25%0% BackReset 00:01 00:00 PlayMute Picture-in-PictureApple AirPlayGoogle CastVRSettingsFullscreen Replay logo After a particularly severe flu season that sickened millions of Americans and sent hundreds of thousands to the hospital, a Bronson physician is urging people to prepare now as the 2026-27 flu season approaches. (Photo illustration by Joe Raedle/Getty Images) Share topics: Flu vaccine H3N2 FDA Influenza A Vaccine update CDC Vaccination rates Seasonal influenza KALAMAZOO, Mich. — After a particularly severe flu season that sickened millions of Americans and sent hundreds of thousands to the hospital, a Bronson physician is urging people to prepare now as the 2026-27 flu season approaches. Dr. William Workman, an internal medicine physician with Bronson and chief of primary care, says a mutated strain of influenza A (H3N2) played a major role in last season’s surge. He believes it could remain the dominant strain this season. “We saw a variant strain come through the hospitals, it was called H3N2 variant. This was kind of a new strain that had evolved recently that caused the increase in office visits and hospitalizations,” Workman said. Weather: Strong to severe storms may bring damaging winds this afternoon and evening The 2025-26 flu season brought significant illness across the United States. Powered By 10 Bronco nation still reeling from UofM loss, joke warrant issued for NCAA Big Ten officials Share Next Stay According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, from Oct. 1, 2025 through Feb. 28, 2026, there were an estimated at least 26 million flu illnesses, 340,000 hospitalizations and 21,000 deaths nationwide. The season was heavily driven by influenza A (H3N2). The CDC reported that 88% of subtyped influenza A-positive specimens were H3N2 during the 2025-2026 season. This was particularly concerning because it emerged after the viruses used to formulate the 2025-2026 vaccine had already been selected. The CDC says the strain was antigenically different from the H3N2 virus included in that season’s vaccine. That kind of viral evolution can make it harder for vaccines to provide as much protection against infection. “When we have the evolution in viruses like that, it does become a little bit difficult because it’s unpredictable. So, then we can’t account for that. So the vaccinations that we have that are coming out are not as effective when we a new variant like that,” Workman said. The Food and Drug Administration updated all three components of the 2026-2027 U.S. flu vaccine. Traffic: Serious crash, vehicle fire closing part of east I-94 in Berrien County The vaccine is designed to protect against three influenza viruses. An H1N1 virus, an H3N2 virus and a B/Victoria lineage virus. Workman says the H3N2 component is particularly important heading into the new season. “So, most importantly, the component of the vaccine will be H3N2. So, being the dominant strain in the population that we suppose, that will help with protection during this season. The other two strains are typical. We have the H3 N1 strain and then we also have a B strain that we protect against as well,” Workman said. The FDA’s annual vaccine selection process is based on surveillance and analysis of influenza viruses circulating around the world and in the United States. Because influenza viruses continually change, vaccine formulations are reviewed and updated each year. Workman said one of the most important things for people to understand is that vaccination does not provide a guarantee that someone will never contract influenza. However, the goal is to reduce the risk of serious illness and complications. “So you can still get the flu with the flu vaccine. You definitely can. But oftentimes, what it’s protecting you against is from severe illness. So even though you might get flu, oftentimes with the vaccination, it protects you against hospitalizations,” Workman said. Workman said people with certain chronic medical conditions are among those he worries about most when flu activity increases. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention: Types of Seasonal Influenza Vaccines “We have to be really careful of. So those are people with type 2 diabetes and ileitis, heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, certain kinds of cancers. Those are a more delicate population and can become sick relatively quickly,” Workman said. Young children and older adults can also face an increased risk of complications from influenza. With children returning to classrooms, Workman said influenza can move quickly through households. He said the incubation period, the time between exposure and developing an infection, can be as short as one to two days. “It can spread quickly, and it’s very virulent. That means that it spreads quickly from one person to another,” Workman said. State News: House Bill 6106 advances in committee to expand Michigan’s school mental health program He recommends that people who are sick stay home and isolate themselves when possible to reduce the risk of exposing people who are more vulnerable. For most people, influenza can cause several days of uncomfortable symptoms. But Workman said there are warning signs that should not be ignored. Those include: Shortness of breath Chest pain Severe weakness Very high fever Workman said shortness of breath is particularly concerning and should prompt someone to seek immediate medical care. Workman said another persistent misconception is that someone can catch influenza from the flu vaccine. “You cannot get the flu from the flu vaccination. It is an inactivated part of the virus and so it is not possible. Likely what happened is either you got the flu vaccination a little bit too late. It takes about two weeks for full effectiveness or it was a strain that was not covered by the vaccine,” Workman said. He also said concerns about serious or long-term effects from vaccination are among the reasons some patients choose not to get vaccinated. The CDC recommends annual flu vaccination for everyone 6 months and older, with some exceptions based on individual circumstances. Local News: Large gas leak causes all day partial closure of Westnedge in Kalamazoo Workman’s biggest concern heading into the new season isn’t necessarily the virus itself, it’s vaccination rates. “I’m most worried about the vaccination rates. It seems we’ve seen in other areas of our community where the vaccinations have rates have decreased with other types of diseases. So I have some concern that we’ll see the same thing with flu vaccination rates, which then leaves our population vulnerable,” Workman said. During the 2025-26 season, CDC estimated that by Feb. 21, about 48% of U.S. children and adolescents ages 6 months through 17 years and 47% of adults 18 and older had received a flu vaccine. analysis.location_and_population: Kalamazoo, Michigan, and the United States. The population includes individuals with chronic medical conditions, young children, and older adults.
analysis.event: The FDA updated the 2026-2027 flu vaccine to include a new H3N2 strain that emerged after the previous season's vaccine was formulated. A Bronson doctor, William Workman, emphasized the importance of preparing for the upcoming flu season due to the potential dominance of the H3N2 variant.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The 2025-2026 flu season caused an estimated 26 million illnesses, 340,000 hospitalizations, and 21,000 deaths in the U.S. The H3N2 variant was the dominant strain, with 88% of subtyped influenza A-positive specimens being H3N2. The new vaccine includes this strain to reduce the risk of severe illness and hospitalizations.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The FDA updated the vaccine based on surveillance and analysis of circulating influenza viruses. The CDC and the Bronson doctor are advising people to prepare for the flu season, emphasizing the importance of vaccination despite its limitations in preventing infection.

analysis.brief_en: The article discusses the FDA's update to the 2026-2027 flu vaccine, which includes a new H3N2 strain that emerged after the previous season's vaccine was formulated. A Bronson doctor, William Workman, highlights the potential for this strain to remain dominant and urges early preparation for the upcoming flu season. The 2025-2026 flu season was particularly severe, with an estimated 26 million illnesses, 340,000 hospitalizations, and 21,000 deaths in the U.S., driven largely by the H3N2 variant. The CDC reports that 88% of subtyped influenza A-positive specimens during that season were H3N2, indicating its significant role. Workman emphasizes that while the vaccine may not guarantee complete protection against infection, it aims to reduce the risk of severe illness and complications, especially for vulnerable groups such as those with chronic medical conditions, young children, and older adults. The article also notes that influenza can spread quickly through households, with an incubation period of one to two days.

The article also notes that influenza can spread quickly through households, with an incubation period of one to two days.

news.title: Don’t mistake H1N1 for routine flu; early signs matter, says doctor - The Tribune
news.rss_summary_html: Don’t mistake H1N1 for routine flu; early signs matter, says doctor  The Tribune
news.excerpt_original: Don’t mistake H1N1 for routine flu; early signs matter, says doctor The Tribune
news.priority_tier_reason: 可信机构来源或已成功抓获正文
news.content_title: Don’t mistake H1N1 for routine flu; early signs matter, says doctor - The Tribune
news.content: H1N1 can begin like an ordinary seasonal viral infection but rapidly progress to pneumonia and breathing difficulties, especially among high-risk groups, says Dr Preeti Salhan, Consultant in Internal Medicine at Fortis Hospital, Jalandhar. Every year around this time, hospitals see the same pattern—high fever, body aches, sore throat and a cough that won’t go away. Most people assume it’s a routine seasonal viral infection, take an over-the-counter medicine and hope to get well at home. But a few days later, many are back at the hospital emergency room struggling to breathe. That second visit is often when the test comes back positive for H1N1 and by then, it’s no longer a simple flu. H1N1 (commonly known as swine flu) and formally designated as seasonal influenza A (H1N1)pdm09 by the National Centre for Disease Control behaves like a regular flu initially, but it can escalate far more rapidly. Doctors emphasise that the main danger isn’t just the virus itself, but it’s how ordinary it looks at first. Almost every patient I see with a serious case tells me the same thing. They thought it was nothing for the first two or three days. By the time patients develop breathlessness, the infection has already spread to the lungs. That initial delay often determines whether someone recovers comfortably at home or ends up needing oxygen support in a hospital bed. Why this flu is different from the others? H1N1 spreads like any other respiratory virus through cough, sneeze and touching contaminated surfaces. While a healthy adult might recover within a week like any standard viral fever, H1N1 can swiftly progress to viral pneumonia in vulnerable individuals. Pregnancy alters both lung capacity and immune function, making H1N1 a serious medical concern for expectant mothers. Chronic conditions like diabetes, heart failure, asthma, or kidney disease put extra strain on the body. An H1N1 infection can cause blood sugar levels to spike and rapidly trigger acute flares of pre-existing illnesses. Symptoms & when to seek immediate care Fever and body aches during the first 24–48 hours are common flu symptoms and generally not a cause for panic. However, seek urgent medical attention if you or a loved one experience any of the following: - Shortness of breath or abnormally rapid breathing - Persistent pain or pressure in the chest - Bluish tint on the lips or fingertips - Sudden dizziness, confusion or difficulty waking up - A sudden worsening of underlying health condition Who is most at risk? You should exercise extra caution if you fall into any of these categories: - Pregnant women (at any trimester) - Children under 5 and adults aged 65 or older - Diabetics (even those with well-managed blood sugar) - Individuals with heart, lung or kidney disease - Anyone on immunosuppressive medications or long-term steroid therapy - Healthcare workers and individuals frequently in crowded public spaces Prevention and early action can save lives Get vaccinated The annual seasonal flu shot is updated every year to target circulating H1N1 strains. It remains the most effective protection against severe illness and hospitalisation. Seek early treatment If prescribed by a doctor, antiviral drugs are most effective when started within the first 48 hours of symptom onset

news.content_original: H1N1 can begin like an ordinary seasonal viral infection but rapidly progress to pneumonia and breathing difficulties, especially among high-risk groups, says Dr Preeti Salhan, Consultant in Internal Medicine at Fortis Hospital, Jalandhar. Every year around this time, hospitals see the same pattern—high fever, body aches, sore throat and a cough that won’t go away. Most people assume it’s a routine seasonal viral infection, take an over-the-counter medicine and hope to get well at home. But a few days later, many are back at the hospital emergency room struggling to breathe. That second visit is often when the test comes back positive for H1N1 and by then, it’s no longer a simple flu. H1N1 (commonly known as swine flu) and formally designated as seasonal influenza A (H1N1)pdm09 by the National Centre for Disease Control behaves like a regular flu initially, but it can escalate far more rapidly. Doctors emphasise that the main danger isn’t just the virus itself, but it’s how ordinary it looks at first. Almost every patient I see with a serious case tells me the same thing. They thought it was nothing for the first two or three days. By the time patients develop breathlessness, the infection has already spread to the lungs. That initial delay often determines whether someone recovers comfortably at home or ends up needing oxygen support in a hospital bed. Why this flu is different from the others? H1N1 spreads like any other respiratory virus through cough, sneeze and touching contaminated surfaces. While a healthy adult might recover within a week like any standard viral fever, H1N1 can swiftly progress to viral pneumonia in vulnerable individuals. Pregnancy alters both lung capacity and immune function, making H1N1 a serious medical concern for expectant mothers. Chronic conditions like diabetes, heart failure, asthma, or kidney disease put extra strain on the body. An H1N1 infection can cause blood sugar levels to spike and rapidly trigger acute flares of pre-existing illnesses. Symptoms & when to seek immediate care Fever and body aches during the first 24–48 hours are common flu symptoms and generally not a cause for panic. However, seek urgent medical attention if you or a loved one experience any of the following: - Shortness of breath or abnormally rapid breathing - Persistent pain or pressure in the chest - Bluish tint on the lips or fingertips - Sudden dizziness, confusion or difficulty waking up - A sudden worsening of underlying health condition Who is most at risk? You should exercise extra caution if you fall into any of these categories: - Pregnant women (at any trimester) - Children under 5 and adults aged 65 or older - Diabetics (even those with well-managed blood sugar) - Individuals with heart, lung or kidney disease - Anyone on immunosuppressive medications or long-term steroid therapy - Healthcare workers and individuals frequently in crowded public spaces Prevention and early action can save lives Get vaccinated The annual seasonal flu shot is updated every year to target circulating H1N1 strains. It remains the most effective protection against severe illness and hospitalisation. Seek early treatment If prescribed by a doctor, antiviral drugs are most effective when started within the first 48 hours of symptom onset

news.content_title: Doctors say they’re filling a void left by CDC on vaccines. Here’s what to know about flu, Covid-19 and RSV this fall
news.content: Pharmacy manager Aylen Amestoy prepares to give a respiratory syncytial virus vaccine at a CVS Pharmacy in Miami in 2025. RSV, flu and Covid-19 vaccines are expected to be available at pharmacies and covered by insurance this fall and winter. Rebecca Blackwell/AP With children back in school and the looming threat of respiratory viruses like Covid-19, influenza and RSV on the horizon, many people may now be wondering how to stay healthy. Typically, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention launches a fall campaign around this time of year, recommending seasonal immunizations such as the flu shot and Covid-19 vaccines. But under the second Trump administration, the agency has mostly been silent this year. The CDC hasn’t issued new recommendations for RSV immunization or Covid-19 vaccines for this season. Last year, the agency updated Covid-19 vaccine guidance to shift away from a broad recommendation, instead saying that patients must consult with a healthcare provider to get the vaccine. Ad Feedback On Tuesday, the agency updated its clinical guidance for the flu shot to follow last year’s recommendations, noting on its website that “the CDC states the recommendations for seasonal influenza vaccination from the July 2025 immunization schedule remain in effect for the 2026-2027 influenza season.” The update does not mention the first mRNA flu vaccine, which was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration last month for use in older adults. To help fill the void, the American Medical Association and the University of Minnesota’s Vaccine Integrity Project launched their own independent reviews of this fall’s vaccines – including those for flu , Covid and RSV – which was published Wednesday in the medical journal JAMA. The review papers helped inform 2026-27 respiratory virus immunization recommendations released Wednesday by several medical groups, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Infectious Diseases Society of America. “For more than 60 years, the United States has benefited from an established federal process for evaluating vaccine evidence and translating that science into recommendations for the American public. At the center of that process were the Centers for Disease Control and its Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, the ACIP,” Dr. Bruce Gellin, board chair of the Vaccine Integrity Project and professor of medicine at Georgetown University, said at a news briefing. “Unfortunately today, the federal government is not fulfilling that responsibility in the way that it historically has. But the need for that work has not disappeared. Influenza, SARS-CoV-2 and the RSV viruses will circulate again this fall and winter,” Gellin said. “Clinicians will still have patients to care for. Parents will still have decisions to make for their children, and older Americans, pregnant women and people with underlying health conditions will still need to know how best to protect themselves,” he said. “We cannot allow the breakdown of a federal process to create a vacuum in evidence-based vaccine guidance.” The US Department of Health and Human Services has not responded to CNN’s request for comment on the groups’ recommendations. The recommendations provide guidance on which fall vaccines are recommended for whom and when is the optimal time to get them. Flu and RSV immunizations are now available at major pharmacies, and updated Covid-19 shots were recently approved by the FDA and are becoming available. “And really reassuringly, insurers have indicated to the major groups that they will cover these respiratory virus immunizations,” Dr. Sarah Nosal, president of the American Academy of Family Physicians, said in the news briefing. “Vaccines are one of medicine’s greatest success stories. They prevent serious illness, reduce hospitalizations and long-term complications and save lives,” Nosal said in a news release. “As federal guidance evolves, the science behind vaccines remains strong. These recommendations are grounded in the latest evidence, informed by public health experts and shaped by what family physicians are seeing every day in their patients.” RSV immunization Who should get it The groups eligible for RSV immunizations include older adults, pregnant people and infants. “People age 50 and older with high-risk conditions, and everyone over 75 years old, should get one dose,” Nosal said. “This is not an annual vaccine. If you got one before, you do not need a new one this year. Getting one should protect you throughout the entire season.” During pregnancy, RSV vaccination is recommended in the third trimester, between weeks 32 and 36. Children younger than 8 months should be immunized against RSV using a monoclonal antibody unless their mother got an RSV vaccination during pregnancy, said Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics. “If the mother’s immunization status is unknown, that child should be immunized,” Racine said in the briefing. He added that children between 8 months and 19 months of age who are in certain high-risk groups for severe disease are also recommended to get the RSV monoclonal antibody. And a single dose of RSV vaccine is recommended for adults who have weakened immune systems. “Immunosuppressed individuals are at higher risk for severe disease than immunocompetent individuals,” Dr. Dan Barouch, director of the Center for Virology and Vaccine Research at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, who was not involved in the new recommendations, said in an email. “The vaccines are also generally less effective in immunosuppressed individuals compared with immunocompetent individuals.” When to get it For older adults, RSV vaccinations are typically recommended in late summer and early fall. The advice slightly changed this year for pregnant people. “ACOG now recommends that pregnant individuals receive a single dose of the maternal RSV vaccine, Abrysvo, from September 1 through March 1 instead of only through January 31,” Dr. Christina Davidson, chief medical officer of the American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists, said in the news briefing. “We made this change because the RSV disease season is now occurring later in the spring, and it is also more severe than it used to be,” Davidson said. “The extension of the eligibility window will help provide pregnant patients and their infants with additional protection.” For infants, the RSV monoclonal antibody is typically recommended around virus season, from October through March. Seasonal flu shots Who should get it Everyone 6 months and older is recommended to get an annual flu shot. “On average, flu vaccines reduce the risk of needing to go to the doctor by 30% to 60%,” Nosal said. “Adults 65 years and older should get an enhanced flu vaccine, one that is high-dose, adjuvanted or recombinant, when it’s available,” she said. “But do not delay your vaccination if that one’s not available.” And for the first time, an mRNA-based flu vaccine is available for use in adults 50 and older. The flu vaccine is also recommended during pregnancy, but pregnant people should avoid the nasal spray version, according to the recommendations. “Pregnant and postpartum people still have a significantly higher risk of developing serious complications from infection compared with non-pregnant people,” Davidson said. “The inactivated or recombinant influenza vaccines remain the only vaccines that are recommended for use in pregnancy in any trimester, so please work with your OB care clinician or pharmacist to get these,” she said. “Most importantly, if you are able to get the vaccine while you are pregnant, the immunity will also, in part, pass on to your baby.” When to get it October is the ideal time to get vaccinated, Nolan said, because “protection wanes throughout the season.” Some providers use the slogan “ flu before boo ” to remind people to get a flu shot before Halloween. Updated Covid-19 vaccines Who should get it Getting an updated Covid-19 vaccine is recommended for adults. “If you’re older than 19, we recommend getting the Covid-19 vaccine,” Nosal said. “This is especially important for people who are 65 years and older, at increased risk for severe Covid infection and those who’ve never received a Covid-19 vaccine,” she said. “For those adults 65 years and older, they should receive a second dose of the updated Covid-19 vaccine six months after that season’s initial dose to help maintain protection as immunity wanes over time.” The vaccine is also recommended for infants between 6 months and 23 months of age, and children in certain high-risk groups or those whose families request vaccination. And for people who are immunocompromised, the annual updated Covid-19 vaccine is recommended for ages 6 months and older. Last year, the CDC recommended Covid-19 vaccines based on conversations with the patient’s healthcare provider, known as shared decision-making, Barouch noted, but the agency “also emphasized that the risk-benefit of the vaccines is most favorable for individuals who are at higher risk of severe disease.” Davidson, of ACOG, said the vaccine is also recommended during pregnancy. “The most important message is this: If you are pregnant, considering pregnancy or are a new or breastfeeding parent, please get your vaccine or your annual booster. All four of the available Covid vaccines are safe for you,” Davidson said. Moderna offers two mRNA shots, Pfizer and BioNTech have another, and Sanofi and Novavax offer a more traditional protein-based version. “A recommendation for the Covid vaccine is based on more than five years of research and millions of administered doses,” Davidson said. “I want to emphasize that the evidence has found no increased risk of miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth, small for gestational age birth or birth defects. The risks of complications from Covid for pregnant people and their babies, however, is high. So please get the vaccine.” When to get it It’s recommended to get the updated vaccine now, but if you have been recently infected with Covid, experts advise waiting four to six months before getting the vaccine. The updated Covid-19 vaccine “targets the most recent strain that’s been circulating, and so if you want to update your protection, that’s the best way to do it,” Dr. Sandra Adamson Fryhofer, president-elect of the American Medical Association, said in the news briefing. “You know, your computer constantly needs to be updated. Well, your immune system, your immunity needs to be constantly updated too,” she said. “You’re going to get your most protection in those first few months after the vaccine. So if you have a big event – if you have to go to a wedding, or if you’re going on some fabulous trip, or you’re going to a fabulous birthday party, or just any birthday party or get-together – think about getting that vaccine a couple of weeks before that event, so you’ll stay healthy and well.” See all topics

news.content: U.S. News World News Korea Regional Review Latin America Region Odd News Entertainment Movies Music TV Sports NFL MLB NBA Soccer Voices Photos News US News World News Entertainment Sports Archive Almanac U.S. News Sept. 2, 2026 / 2:33 PM Doctors release vaccine recommendations for RSV, influenza, COVID-19 By Lisa Hornung Medical groups have released vaccine recommendations this fall in lieu of guidance from the CDC. File Photo by Javier Aparico/EPA Sept. 2 (UPI) -- A group of medical organizations has released guidance on fall vaccinations against respiratory illnesses. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention usually launches a fall campaign to recommend seasonal vaccines for diseases like RSV, influenza and COVID-19. This year, however, the agency has not issued its updated recommendations for the respiratory virus season. In March, the American Academy of Pediatrics won a lawsuit against the federal government that blocked Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. from overhauling the childhood vaccine schedule. Kennedy and President Donald Trump have said that children get too many vaccines and have reduced the number of vaccines routinely recommended. They have also linked vaccines to autism, which has been proven untrue by research. In response, the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, the American Academy of Family Physicians, the Infectious Diseases Society of America each issued guidelines for fall immunizations. They based those guidelines on research from the American Medical Association and the University of Minnesota's Vaccine Integrity Project Last year, the CDC changed the COVID-19 recommendations to say that patients should talk to their own doctors. On Tuesday, the agency said, "the CDC states the recommendations for seasonal influenza vaccination from the July 2025 immunization schedule remain in effect for the 2026-2027 influenza season." It doesn't mention the new mRNA flu vaccine, approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration last month. "For more than 60 years, the United States has benefited from an established federal process for evaluating vaccine evidence and translating that science into recommendations for the American public. At the center of that process were the Centers for Disease Control and its Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, the ACIP," CNN reported Dr. Bruce Gellin, board chair of the Vaccine Integrity Project and professor of medicine at Georgetown University, said at a press briefing. "Unfortunately today, the federal government is not fulfilling that responsibility in the way that it historically has. But the need for that work has not disappeared. Influenza, SARS-CoV-2 [COVID-19] and the RSV viruses will circulate again this fall and winter," Gellin said. "We cannot allow the breakdown of a federal process to create a vacuum in evidence-based vaccine guidance," he added. Dr. Sarah Nosal, president of the American Academy of Family Physicians, said in the news briefing that insurance companies have indicated they will cover the vaccines. "Vaccines are one of medicine's greatest success stories. They prevent serious illness, reduce hospitalizations and long-term complications and save lives," Nosal said in a press release. "As federal guidance evolves, the science behind vaccines remains strong. These recommendations are grounded in the latest evidence, informed by public health experts and shaped by what family physicians are seeing every day in their patients." (ADAM LAM/CHINA DAILY) Amid the ongoing influenza season and the return of thousands of students to classrooms across Hong Kong last week, health authorities are urging the public to receive their influenza vaccinations promptly. The Centre for Health Protection (CHP) of the Department of Health (DH) has announced the commencement of the 2026/27 Seasonal Influenza Vaccination (SIV) Programmes on Sept 17. ALSO READ: HK residents urged to get flu jab with three more children infected These initiatives include the SIV School Outreach Programme (SIVSOP), the Residential Care Home Vaccination Programme, and the Vaccination Subsidy Scheme (VSS), all designed to safeguard the health of individuals and their families. Eligible individuals can access free or subsidized vaccinations through these initiatives. China Daily's Adam Lam took the photos on Monday. Summary Singapore's influenza positivity rate increased to 36.6% from August 16 to 22, compared to 24.0% the previous week in 2026. The Communicable Diseases Agency reports no indication of increased severity despite the rise in cases. Individuals at higher risk are advised to receive annual influenza vaccinations. First Published: Wednesday, 02 Sep 2026 9:25 AM MYT × Subscribe to Newsletter Subscribe SINGAPORE, Sept 2 — Singapore recorded an increase in influenza cases, with the positivity rate rising to 36.6 per cent in the week from Aug 16 to 22, 2026, compared with 24.0 per cent in the previous week. The Communicable Diseases Agency (CDA), however, said there was no indication that the infections were more severe than usual. “The current influenza positivity levels remain below last year’s peak of 43.9 per cent observed in January 2025. CDA is monitoring the situation,” it said in a statement on Tuesday. According to the CDA, Singapore national surveillance data indicate that seasonal influenza viruses circulate throughout the year, with periods of higher activity typically observed between May and August and December and March. These bimodal peaks broadly coincide with the Northern and Southern Hemisphere winter periods, but the timing may vary from year to year due to factors such as international travel and population mixing patterns, it added. The agency also advised individuals at higher risk of developing severe influenza infections, and vulnerable groups with underlying medical conditions, to receive their influenza vaccinations at least once a year. — Bernama FURTHER QUESTIONS? First Published: Wednesday, 02 Sep 2026 9:25 AM MYT × Subscribe to Newsletter Subscribe SINGAPORE, Sept 2 — Singapore recorded an increase in influenza cases, with the positivity rate rising to 36.6 per cent in the week from Aug 16 to 22, 2026, compared with 24.0 per cent in the previous week. The Communicable Diseases Agency (CDA), however, said there was no indication that the infections were more severe than usual. “The current influenza positivity levels remain below last year’s peak of 43.9 per cent observed in January 2025. CDA is monitoring the situation,” it said in a statement on Tuesday. According to the CDA, Singapore national surveillance data indicate that seasonal influenza viruses circulate throughout the year, with periods of higher activity typically observed between May and August and December and March. These bimodal peaks broadly coincide with the Northern and Southern Hemisphere winter periods, but the timing may vary from year to year due to factors such as international travel and population mixing patterns, it added. The agency also advised individuals at higher risk of developing severe influenza infections, and vulnerable groups with underlying medical conditions, to receive their influenza vaccinations at least once a year. — Bernama FURTHER QUESTIONS? news.title_zh: 新加坡流感病例增加,阳性率升至36.6pc,卫生机构监测疫情 - 马来邮报
news.source_body_en: Singapore has seen an increase in influenza cases, with the positivity rate rising to 36.6% in the week from August 16 to 22, 2026, compared to 24.0% in the previous week. This increase was reported by the Communicable Diseases Agency (CDA), which emphasized that there is no indication of heightened severity. The CDA noted that current positivity levels are still below the historical peak of 43.9% recorded in January 2025. While no specific case or death numbers were provided, the agency is actively monitoring the situation and has advised high-risk individuals and those with underlying medical conditions to get their annual influenza vaccinations. The report was first published on September 2, 2026, and highlights the seasonal nature of influenza in Singapore, with activity typically peaking between May and August and December and March. The CDA also mentioned that factors such as international travel and population mixing can influence the timing of these peaks.

news.content: 澎湃号·湃客 > 流感流行提前?第35周数据给出信号 儿科严医生 复旦大学儿科学博士 2026-09-05 18:06 上海 2026 年 9 月 3 日,中国疾控中心发布了第 35 周(8 月 24 日 至 8 月 30 日)全国急性呼吸道传染病哨点监测数据。同日,国家流感中心也发布了《流感监测周报》。 第 35 周最显著的变化是:新冠病毒核酸阳性率大幅下降(- 3.7%),而流感病毒核酸阳性率继续攀升(+ 1.3%)。 两者在第 35 周完成交叉,流感跃居首位(17.7%)。 第 35 周《流感监测周报》显示: 第 35 周,南方省份流感病毒核酸阳性率已经达到 20.8%,以甲流H3N2驱动。而第 34 周是 18.3%。 至于其他常见呼吸道病原体,目前主要还是小幅波动,还没有看到明显的流行态势。 第 35 周数据反映的还是开学前的情况。 随着学校和幼儿园陆续开学,部分常见呼吸道病原体的传播应该会加快。 2026年第 35 周,流感核酸阳性率17.7%,而去年同期(2025年第 35 周),流感核酸阳性率仅2.4%。看上去,2026年的流感季像是“提前了”。 但更合理的解释也许是:南方夏季流感还没有完全退下去,B(Victoria)之后,H3N2 亚分支又开始接力上升;而既往,中国南方部分地区就存在H3N2夏季流行的特点。 几股力量叠加,使得今年8月的流感阳性率明显高于去年同期。 至于这是否意味着今年全国范围内秋冬流感季真正提前了,目前无法给出确切结论,要看开学后3~4周南北方的走势。 不论如何,对于南方地区的适龄人群,我建议:流感疫苗应尽快接种,不必观望。 参考来源 https://www.chinacdc.cn/jksj/jksj04_14275/202609/t20260903_1839779.html https://www.chinacdc.cn/jksj/jksj04_14249/202609/t20260903_1839747.html https://journals.plos.org/plospathogens/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.ppat.1011046 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9501233/ 原标题:《流感流行提前?第35周数据给出信号》 阅读原文 特别声明 本文为澎湃号作者或机构在澎湃新闻上传并发布,仅代表该作者或机构观点,不代表澎湃新闻的观点或立场,澎湃新闻仅提供信息发布平台。申请澎湃号请用电脑访问https://renzheng.thepaper.cn。 14 相关推荐 尿液出现这种颜色,可能是癌症信号 肿瘤专科医生 14小时前 别等确诊糖尿病才后悔!血糖超标的信号,年轻人也要警惕 腾讯医典 23小时前 儿童心理咨询:脾气暴躁、易怒,可能是孩子发出的求助信号 听说吧心理咨询 15小时前 中疾控:建议所有6月龄及以上且无接种禁忌的人接种流感疫苗 绿政公署 4天前 24小时最热 00:34 驳船往长江倾倒黑色固体“十秒清空一艘船”?武汉市生态环境局:已赴现场调查 锋线视频 20小时前 458评 郭德纲歪曲篡改抗战歌曲,武汉文旅局发布处理通报 直击现场 12小时前 216评 星宇股份发布近期调岗减员错误行为的相关情况及整改措施 10%公司 17小时前 398评 起售价过万!小米18 Fold发布,雷军谈造芯:只要开始追赶,小米就走在赢的路上 10%公司 9小时前 37评 央媒调查一企业私设码头:多头监管4年关不掉,现场执法被暴力阻挠 直击现场 22小时前 97评 你有权知道更多 下载澎湃新闻客户端 下载APP 脱离遥控器,人形机器人全自主格斗!宇树科技又公布新进展 马上评|冒充公职人员挂账消费何以能得逞? analysis.brief_en: Influenza activity in China showed early season signals during week 35 (August 24‐30, 2026), with nucleic acid positivity rising to 17.7%, up from 2.4% the previous year, according to the China CDC and National Influenza Center. Southern provinces recorded a positivity rate of 20.8%, driven by H3N2, while national rates crossed the 17% threshold, suggesting a possible early influenza season. No specific case or death counts were reported, and the article did not assign a quantified risk level. In response, health authorities advised all individuals aged six months and older without contraindications to receive the influenza vaccine promptly, emphasizing that vaccination should not be delayed. Uncertainty persists regarding the true timing of the season, as post‐school opening trends in the coming weeks will clarify whether the observed rise reflects an actual early onset or merely pre‐season fluctuations.

华人号 2026-03-13 17:01 阅读量:1.4万+ 华人号:华人头条-阿根廷 华人头条阿根廷3月13日讯/Cl:阿根廷2026年流感疫苗接种活动将于本周三在全国启动。与去年相比,今年的接种计划提前了三周,目的是在呼吸道病毒高发季节到来之前,为重点人群建立免疫保护。同时,目前正在传播的一种新的甲型流感A(H3N2)变异株具有更高的传播性。 阿根廷卫生部(Ministerio de Salud)表示,此次接种活动的目标是为可能出现并发症或重症的群体提供更强的免疫保护,并减轻流感对医疗系统的压力。 这一决定与近年来呼吸道病毒季节提前有关,同时也与新的甲型流感A(H3N2)变异株传播有关,该病毒具有更强的传染能力。 通过提前规划和物流安排,国家卫生部门共采购了8,160,000剂疫苗,其中包括: 4,700,000剂成人流感疫苗 2,300,000剂佐剂型流感疫苗(aTIV) 1,160,000剂儿童流感疫苗 疫苗从2月初开始分发至各省。目前已向全国各地发放超过180万剂,预计在3月底前还将追加发放1,018,640剂。 与此同时,阿根廷卫生部(Ministerio de Salud)还制定了一项综合准备策略,包括对全国医疗团队进行培训,并发布《2026年流感疫苗接种技术指南》(Lineamientos Técnicos de Vacunación Antigripal 2026)。该文件详细说明了接种目标人群和优先群体、疫苗成分、国家免疫计划中的接种方案以及具体实施标准,以确保全国范围内统一、规范地开展接种工作。 2026年流感疫苗接种对象 建议接种流感疫苗的人群包括: 6个月至24个月的儿童 医务人员 65岁及以上老年人 孕妇 产妇(若在怀孕期间未接种,可在出院后10天内接种) 任何年龄但具有基础疾病或风险因素的人群 疫苗可在全国各地的公立医院、卫生中心和疫苗接种点免费接种,并且可以与国家免疫计划(Calendario Nacional)中的其他疫苗同时接种。 卫生部门还呼吁公众积极接种,并强调:“国家免疫计划中的所有疫苗都是安全的,经过多年验证,有科学证据支持,并且能够有效预防疾病。” (完) 阿根廷卫生部(Ministerio de Salud)表示,此次接种活动的目标是为可能出现并发症或重症的群体提供更强的免疫保护,并减轻流感对医疗系统的压力。 这一决定与近年来呼吸道病毒季节提前有关,同时也与新的甲型流感A(H3N2)变异株传播有关,该病毒具有更强的传染能力。 通过提前规划和物流安排,国家卫生部门共采购了8,160,000剂疫苗,其中包括: 4,700,000剂成人流感疫苗 2,300,000剂佐剂型流感疫苗(aTIV) 1,160,000剂儿童流感疫苗 疫苗从2月初开始分发至各省。目前已向全国各地发放超过180万剂,预计在3月底前还将追加发放1,018,640剂。 与此同时,阿根廷卫生部(Ministerio de Salud)还制定了一项综合准备策略,包括对全国医疗团队进行培训,并发布《2026年流感疫苗接种技术指南》(Lineamientos Técnicos de Vacunación Antigripal 2026)。该文件详细说明了接种目标人群和优先群体、疫苗成分、国家免疫计划中的接种方案以及具体实施标准,以确保全国范围内统一、规范地开展接种工作。 2026年流感疫苗接种对象 建议接种流感疫苗的人群包括: 6个月至24个月的儿童 医务人员 65岁及以上老年人 孕妇 产妇(若在怀孕期间未接种,可在出院后10天内接种) 任何年龄但具有基础疾病或风险因素的人群 疫苗可在全国各地的公立医院、卫生中心和疫苗接种点免费接种,并且可以与国家免疫计划(Calendario Nacional)中的其他疫苗同时接种。 卫生部门还呼吁公众积极接种,并强调:“国家免疫计划中的所有疫苗都是安全的,经过多年验证,有科学证据支持,并且能够有效预防疾病。” (完) supplementary_news.content: Avian Flu Diary Covering Pandemic and Seasonal Flu, Emerging Infectious Diseases, public health, community & Individual preparedness. NOTE: All AFD blogs are written by a human - any mistakes are solely mine. Monday, September 07, 2026 Pathogen's Progress H5 Affected States & Provinces June 2015 #19,326 Prior to 2021, North America had only had one brush with the Asian-origin HPAI H5 virus; a reassorted H5N8 subtype which appeared in South Korea in January of 2014 before beginning a world tour. It crossed the north Pacific - carried by migratory birds - the following fall, arriving in the Pacific Northwest in December 2014, sparking the first HPAI H5 epizootic in the United States and Canada (see map above). That H5Nx virus, however, disappeared completely the following summer, apparently still ill-suited for long-term carriage by wild and migratory birds (see PNAS: The Enigma Of Disappearing HPAI H5 In North American Migratory Waterfowl). That limitation would evaporate in the summer of 2016 when H5N8 reassorted into a far more robust threat (probably in China or Siberia) - arriving in Europe in October - and sparking their biggest (at that time) epizootic on record. EID Journal: Reassorted HPAI H5N8 Clade 2.3.4.4. - Germany 2016). This new H5N8 was not only deadlier to some bird species, it was more easily carried by others, increasing its range and impact dramatically over the next 6 months. We also saw this virus spin off several short-lived subtypes, including H5N5, H5N3, and H5N9. Over the winter of 2016-17, this H5N8 virus spread from Europe, into the Middle East, and then North Africa. By late spring, 2017, it had crossed the equator for the first time, and set up shop in South Africa, making it the most successfully disseminated HPAI H5 virus we'd seen. A European H5N6 briefly appeared in 2018, but H5N8 held on until a new, reassorted H5N1 virus appeared in Europe in 2020, and began to supplant H5N8. Unlike previous H5Nx incarnations, this new H5N1 showed an increased affinity for infecting mammals, and a much wider avian host range (see DEFRA: The Unprecedented `Order Shift' In Wild Bird H5N1 Positives In Europe & The UK). By 2022 this `new and improved' H5N1 virus had crossed both the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, spreading first to North America, followed by South America, the Antarctic, and most recently (2026) into Australia/New Zealand. While avian flu activity still decreased during the hotter months, no longer did HPAI H5 disappear completely each summer. It could be maintained (at low levels) in local birds, livestock, small mammals, and likely even the environment. All of which makes the HPAI H5 threat of today far different from what it was even a decade ago. The H5N1 virus of today has expanded not only its geographic range, but its host range as well. And it isn't done evolving. Since its arrival in 2021, the H5Nx virus has diversified into more than 100 distinct genotypes in North America alone, with scores of others emerging around the globe. A few notable North American examples include: In late 2023 a new B3.13 genotype emerged that could efficiently infect dairy cattle while mildly infecting dozens of humans Last fall we saw 3 new genotypes emerge (D1.1, D1.2, D1.3), with D1.1 producing more severe illness in humans. In October 2024 Canada experienced a multi-farm outbreak of emerging N1 genotype of H5N1 that was highly resistant to NAI antivirals (carrying the H275Y mutation) These variants illustrate just how quickly (and dramatically) the avian `fluscape' can change, and we generally see those changes in the fall, when migratory birds - which spent their summers in their high latitude roosting areas - return. A 2016 study (see Sci Repts.: Southward Autumn Migration Of Waterfowl Facilitates Transmission Of HPAI H5N1), suggests that waterfowl pick up new HPAI viruses in the spring (likely from poultry or terrestrial birds) on their northbound trip to their summer breeding spots - where they spread and potentially evolve - and then redistribute them on their southbound journey the following fall. Our own Arctic Refuge, where more than 200 bird species spend their summers, serves as a central hub, and funnels migratory birds south via all four North American Flyways. While this fall's HPAI viruses could be similar to what we saw last year - they might include new, potentially game-changing, genotypes - which could either increase or decrease their threat. Evolution is a double-edged sword, and what it adds it can also take away. But the trajectory of H5N1 over the past 4+ years has been towards more mammalian adaptation, and increased host range. We've also seen reports of H5N5 activity above the Arctic Circle (see Norwegian Veterinary Institute Reports Another HPAI H5N5 Infected Polar Bear on Svalbard Island), and H5N5 claimed the life of a Washington state bird keeper last fall. The APPA estimates `Eleven (11) million U.S. households own backyard chickens (a 28% increase from 2023)', yet a recent survey (see MMWR: Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices Regarding Avian Influenza Among Owners of Backyard Flocks) found significant gaps in their knowledge of dealing with avian flu. While no one can predict with any confidence what HPAI will look like later this fall, the one thing we can be sure of is the 2026 fall southbound migration has already begun, and the time to prepare for its arrival grows shorter with every passing day. And if recent history is any guide, we should be preparing for additional surprises. Sunday, September 06, 2026 CDC Update: Flu Levels Remain Low, But COVID Increasing Across the U.S. Last Week This Week #19,325 Last week, after a summer of low COVID activity reported in the United States, we looked at Low But Increasing COVID reports across the nation. At that time, wastewater testing in 8 states indicated increased activity, while this week (see graphic above) the number of states has risen to 11. At the same time, the percentage of positive tests for COVID has jumped from 5.3 last week to 6.2 this week. Still low, but edging higher. The CDC's weekly summary reads: Testing, and reporting, of COVID cases remain low, and so the CDC's Nowcast is unable provide us with much in the way of details on this summer's variants. Last month the FDA approved a new JN.1 lineage XFG subvariant COVID vaccine (see CIDRAP FDA approves new COVID vaccines) which should be available later this fall. Currently, influenza and RSV are reportedly at very low levels (see chart below), but with fall approaching, those numbers are expected to rise in the months ahead. As reported a little over a week ago (see Japan MHLW Reports Unusually Early Start to the Fall Flu Season) a few countries in the Northern Hemisphere are already reporting substantial flu, even as the virus continues in the Southern Hemisphere. Admittedly, every flu season is different, and it is not unusual to see vastly different flu seasons in different parts of the world. So flu's early arrival in Japan may not be a harbinger for North America or Europe. This year's fall flu vaccines have been updated to reflect recent antigenic changes observed in all 3 seasonal flu types (see WHO Recommendations for Influenza Vaccine Composition for the 2026-2027 Northern Hemisphere Influenza Season). While no flu vaccine can promise 100% protection, it – along with practicing good flu hygiene (washing hands, wearing face masks in crowded indoor spaces, covering coughs, & staying home if sick) – remains your best strategy for avoiding the flu and staying healthy this winter. For some more reasons to consider getting the flu vaccine, you may wish to revisit: Eurosurveillance: Influenza Vaccination Attenuates Acute Myocardial Infarction and Stroke Risk Following Influenza Infection Nature: Influenza Vaccination & Major Cardiovascular Risk: a Systematic Review & Meta-Analysis The Lancet: Influenza Vaccine to Reduce Adverse Vascular Events in Patients with Heart Failure AHA: Study Shows Flu Shots Reduce Deaths From Heart Failure Saturday, September 05, 2026 #NPM26: Preparing For An El Niño Winter Credit NOAA Note: This is the 5th day of National Preparedness Month. Follow this year’s campaign on Twitter by searching for the #NatlPrep #BeReady or #PrepMonth hashtags. This month, as part of NPM26, I’ll be rerunning some updated preparedness essays, along with some new ones. #19,324 Two years ago I was forced to evacuate (for the 3rd time in 10 years) from my west-central Florida home due to the approach of hurricane Milton, which passed 50-60 miles to my south. While I live roughly 40 miles inland, and at a high (for Florida) elevation, we saw prolonged hurricane force winds, massive tree damage, and - thanks to 14" of rain in a few hours - a 500 year-flood. It took 4 days for the water to recede enough for me to return home. Luckily I had a `disaster buddy' who took me and my cat in for the duration. I was lucky, my home wasn't flooded, although some only a hundred yards away were. It took 4 days to get power back on, and a week to get internet (see Signs of Life). While my home took substantial wind damage, it was inland flooding that caused the worst damage to my community. Now, imagine that sort of rain dump happening - perhaps repeatedly - this winter in California. That's the growing concern for state officials (see ABC-7 News 'Super El Niño' strengthens, triggering preparations for possible flooding in LA County). Depending on the intensity, duration, and frequency of such storms, it could even lead to an ARkStorm event, which we first looked at 15 years ago in ARkStorm: California’s other "Big One". While it sounds like the plot from a bad made-for-cable Sci Fi film, this actually comes from the USGS Multi Hazards Demonstration Project (MHDP) analysis of a winter storm scenario with historical precedence. From the USGS website: Experts have designed a large, scientifically realistic meteorological event followed by an examination of the secondary hazards (for example, landslides and flooding), physical damages to the built environment, and social and economic consequences. The hypothetical storm depicted here would strike the U.S. West Coast and be similar to the intense California winter storms of 1861 and 1862 that left the central valley of California impassible. The storm is estimated to produce precipitation that in many places exceeds levels only experienced on average once every 500 to 1,000 years. USGS Video On ARkStorm We returned to this topic in 2022's California's ARkStorm Scenario Revisited, after the USGS released an updated assessment; one that suggested that as the climate grows hotter and dryer, it increases the odds of seeing another catastrophic ARkStorm event. Climate change is increasing the risk of a California megaflood XINGYING HUANG AND DANIEL L. SWAIN SCIENCE ADVANCES 12 Aug 2022 Vol 8, Issue 32 DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.abq0995 Abstract Despite the recent prevalence of severe drought, California faces a broadly underappreciated risk of severe floods. Here, we investigate the physical characteristics of “plausible worst case scenario” extreme storm sequences capable of giving rise to “megaflood” conditions using a combination of climate model data and high-resolution weather modeling. Using the data from the Community Earth System Model Large Ensemble, we find that climate change has already doubled the likelihood of an event capable of producing catastrophic flooding, but larger future increases are likely due to continued warming. We further find that runoff in the future extreme storm scenario is 200 to 400% greater than historical values in the Sierra Nevada because of increased precipitation rates and decreased snow fraction. These findings have direct implications for flood and emergency management, as well as broader implications for hazard mitigation and climate adaptation activities. (Continue . . . ) This is an extreme scenario - and remains a low probability event despite this winter's El Niño - but even something less severe could cause considerable damage, and potentially loss of life. So, the question is, how ready are you and your family for severe weather this winter? The LA County website advises: LA County is preparing its flood control and emergency response systems now. Crews are inspecting and maintaining dams, debris basins, channels, storm drains, and pump stations; monitoring burn areas, hillsides, and other areas at risk of flooding and debris flows; and preparing for evacuations, emergency shelter, and other storm response. County teams are also preparing to assist people experiencing homelessness, older adults, and others who may need additional help during severe weather. Here’s what residents can do now: Sign up for emergency alerts: Go to alert.lacounty.gov to receive emergency notifications, including evacuation warnings and orders. Know the risks where you live: If you are near a hillside, canyon, recent burn area, or area that can flood, learn your flood and mudflow risk before a storm. Make an evacuation plan: Know where you will go and how you will get there if you need to leave quickly. Have supplies ready: Keep enough food, water, medications, and other essentials for up to 10 days. Prepare your home: Clear gutters, downspouts, and storm drains, fix roof leaks, and get sandbags before heavy rain is in the forecast. Consider flood insurance: Standard homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage. Flood insurance is separate and can take at least 30 days to go into effect. Need help with mud or debris flow risk? Call LA County Public Works at 1-800-933-0930 to speak with an engineer. Know someone experiencing homelessness who needs help? Visit homeless.lacounty.gov/get-help/ But it isn't just California that could be impacted by a strong El Niño. Here in Florida - where we are enjoying the quietest Atlantic Hurricane Season in recent memory - we've a history of seeing strong winter storms during El Niño years, including the tornado outbreak of 1998 which killed 42 people. Predicting exactly where unusual or severe weather will occur this winter due to El Niño is impossible, but generally, the jet stream across the United States shifts storm tracks to the southern tier of states. While this doesn't guarantee that other areas will get a free ride this winter, it does suggest that California may be unusually wet, and ice storms and blizzards may be more likely to develop across the deep south this coming winter. Exactly where that may happen is unknowable, but five years ago (Feb 2021) 3 successive winter storms swept across Texas, Louisiana, and Oklahoma, causing the worst collapse of the Texas energy grid on record (see Texas: The Latest - But Not The Last - Grid Down Crisis). At least 4.5 million homes were without power during a week of bitter winter temperatures, resulting in hundreds of deaths and tens of billions of dollars of damage (see City of Austin & Travis County 2021 WINTER STORM URI AFTER-ACTION REVIEW). While I can't tell you where the next natural disaster will strike, or how bad it will be, being prepared for whatever comes is your best defense. So, if the grid goes down, or flood waters rise, or the ground begins to shake . . . do you already have? A battery operated NWS Emergency Radio to find out what was going on, and to get vital instructions from emergency officials A decent first-aid kit, so that you can treat injuries Enough non-perishable food and water on hand to feed and hydrate your family (including pets) for the duration A way to provide light when the grid is down. A way to cook safely without electricity A way to purify or filter water A way to handle basic sanitation and waste disposal. A way to stay cool (fans) or warm when the power is out. A small supply of cash to use in case credit/debit machines are not working An emergency plan, including meeting places, emergency out-of-state contact numbers, a disaster buddy, and in case you must evacuate, a bug-out bag Spare supply of essential prescription medicines that you or your family may need A way to entertain yourself, or your kids, during a prolonged blackout If not, you've got some important work to do. A good place to get started is by visiting Ready.gov. Friday, September 04, 2026 #NatlPrep: 75% of Americans At Risk Of Experiencing A Damaging Earthquake Note: This is the 4th day of National Preparedness Month. This month, as part of NPM26, I’ll be rerunning some updated preparedness essays, along with some new ones. #19,323 Over the past 3 months, in addition to hundreds of mild-to-moderate earthquakes, the world has seen 3 devastating seismic events: In early June, the Philippines was struck by a 7.8 quake offshore of Mindanao, killing more than 100 people, and damaging more than 100 thousand homes. Two weeks later Venezuela was struck by twin quakes (7.2 and 7.5) - 39 seconds apart - killing more than 6500 people, and destroying tens of thousands of buildings. Three weeks after that (August 10th) Colombia was hit by a 7.4 quake, killing > 330 people, and causing massive infrastructure collapse. While we like to think that these sorts of events can't happen here in the United States, Canada, or Europe, the truth is more sobering. In 2006 the USGS calculated that earthquakes posed a significant risk to 75 million Americans living in 39 States. A 2015 study, published in the journal Earthquake Spectra, nearly doubled – to 143 million - the number of Americans who live or work in areas susceptible to potentially damaging ground shaking (see USGS: Nearly Half Of U.S. Population Exposed to Potentially Damaging Earthquakes). supplementary_news.content: 顶部 首页 首页 小雨 / 18° 隐私 5岁男童确诊流感,情况严重!香港披露详情!中疾控呼吁:这8类人群优先接种疫苗 南方都市报 9月1日,香港卫生署卫生防护中心录得一宗儿童感染甲型流感的严重个案。该中心呼吁市民在9月17日季节性流感疫苗接种计划展开后尽快接种季节性流感疫苗,以保障自己和家人健康。 据香港特区政府新闻公报网披露,个案涉及一名有长期病患的5岁男童。他自8月30日起出现发烧、咳嗽和气促,同日被带到私家医院求医。由于他出现呼吸困难,被转介至玛丽医院儿童深切治疗部留医。他的呼吸道样本经化验后,证实对甲型流感病毒呈阳性反应,临床诊断为甲型流感并发严重肺炎。病人目前仍然在儿童深切治疗部留医,情况严重。 该中心初步调查显示,男童于潜伏期内没有外游。他的其中一名家居接触者近日曾出现轻微上呼吸道症状,病况轻微,无需入院。 该中心总监徐乐坚医生表示:“本港自六月底进入流感季节,流感活跃程度在七月至八月中持续攀升。根据最新的监测数据,流感活跃程度仍处于高水平。由于近月社区的流感传播广泛,感染人数大幅增加,严重个案亦随之上升。我们预料开学初期流感仍会持续活跃,而学校亦可能出现流感爆发个案,因此学校和家长必须提高警惕并采取预防措施。” 徐乐坚医生呼吁全港学校及家长和中心通力合作,尽早完成同意程序,早日安排学童接种流感疫苗。” 展开剩余 77 % 徐乐坚医生提醒家长,儿童患上流感,情况可能迅速恶化,家长必须注意患病儿童的身体状况,一旦发现病童情况转差,例如出现呼吸急促、喘鸣、咀唇发紫、胸痛、神智模糊、持续发烧或抽搐等,必须立即前往急症室求医。市民一旦出现呼吸道病征,亦应尽快就医,若与高危群组人士(如儿童、长者及有长期病患或免疫力低等)同住,在家中亦应佩戴外科口罩,以减低高危群组受感染的机会。其他有效减少疾病传播方法包括保持家居卫生,经常清洁和消毒常接触的表面,注意手部卫生和保持室内空气流通。 中疾控:流感活动近期小幅上升 根据中国疾控中心发布的第35周全国急性呼吸道传染病哨点监测情况(详情),2026年8月24日—8月30日,全国哨点医院门急诊流感样病例呼吸道样本检测阳性率前三位病原体为流感病毒(17.7%)、新型冠状病毒(15.8%)、鼻病毒(2.8%)。 其中,新型冠状病毒检测阳性率呈下降趋势,总体上处于中流行水平,流感活动近期小幅上升,主要为B(Victoria)系和A(H3N2)亚型流感病毒,A(H3N2)亚型占比上升,南方省份检测阳性率处于中流行水平波动,北方省份处于流行间期水平,15~59岁病例组检测阳性率最高。 南都资料图 中疾控:优先推荐这八类人群接种疫苗 流行性感冒(简称“流感”)是流感病毒引起的急性呼吸道传染病,在我国属于法定丙类传染病。流感病毒抗原性易变,传染性强,传播速度快,在学校、托幼机构和养老院等人群聚集的场所易发生暴发疫情。人群对流感病毒普遍易感,老年人、婴幼儿、慢性病患者和孕妇等人群感染流感后易出现严重并发症。流感冬春季高发,其季节性流行造成较为严重的健康危害和经济负担。 每年接种流感疫苗是预防流感最为经济有效的措施。2026—2027年度我国上市的三价流感疫苗包括三价灭活疫苗(IIV3)和三价减毒活疫苗(LAIV3),其中 IIV3 有裂解疫苗和亚单位疫苗,可用于 6 月龄及以上人群,包括 0.25 mL 和 0.5 mL两种剂型;LAIV3 适用于 3—17 岁人群,每剂次 0.2 mL。 为更好地推动我国流感疫苗的预防接种,中国疾病预防控制中心组织国家免疫规划技术工作组流感疫苗专题工作组收集和整理国内外流感和流感疫苗相关的最新研究进展和科学证据,形成了《中国流感疫苗预防接种技术指南(2026—2027)》(以下简称“指南”)。 本指南建议所有6月龄及以上且无接种禁忌的人接种流感疫苗。结合流感疫情形势和多病共防的防控策略,尽可能降低流感的危害,优先推荐以下重点和高风险人群接种: 1. 医务人员,包括临床救治人员、公共卫生人员、卫生检疫人员等; 2. 60岁及以上的老年人; 3. 罹患一种或多种慢性病者; 4. 养老机构、长期护理机构、福利院等人群聚集场所脆弱人群及员工; 5. 6月龄及以上—5岁以下的儿童; 6. 6月龄以下婴儿的家庭成员和看护人员; 7. 托幼机构、中小学校、监管场所等重点场所人群; 8. 孕妇。 对于6月龄及以上—9岁以下儿童,若该年龄段儿童既往未接种过流感疫苗,首次接种流感病毒灭活疫苗时,应接种2剂次(2剂次选择同一厂家同种疫苗),间隔≥4周;若该年龄段儿童既往接种过流感疫苗,则本年度建议接种1剂次。 若该年龄段儿童接种流感病毒减毒活疫苗,无论既往是否接种过流感疫苗,仅需接种1剂次。 对于9岁及以上儿童和成人,无论既往是否接种过流感疫苗,仅需接种1剂次。 通常接种流感疫苗2—4周后,可产生具有保护水平的抗体。我国各地每年流感活动高峰出现的时间和持续时间不同,为保证受种者在流感高发季前获得免疫保护,各地在疫苗供应后应尽快安排接种工作,最好在当地流感流行季前完成接种。综合我国南、北方的流感流行特点,通常在 11 月份左右进入冬春季流感流行季,建议在 9—10 月完成接种;即使此时间段内未完成接种,整个流行季也都可以接种。同一流感流行季,按照免疫程序完成全程接种的人员,无需重复接种。 Free web novels for online reading. 评论 全部 还没有人评论过,快来抢首评 抢首评 推荐阅读 温碧霞本色出演,堪称颜值巅峰之作,看得热血沸腾 文娱江湖 2026.8.12 1535.3万+
